prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN)  -- Husbands are allowed to slap their wives if they spend lavishly, a Saudi judge said recently during a seminar on domestic violence, Saudi media reported Sunday. It is OK to slap Saudi women who spend too much, a judge has told an audience. Arab News, a Saudi English-language daily newspaper based in Riyadh, reported that Judge Hamad Al-Razine said that "if a person gives SR 1,200 [$320] to his wife and she spends 900 riyals [$240] to purchase an abaya [the black cover that women in Saudi Arabia must wear] from a brand shop and if her husband slaps her on the face as a reaction to her action, she deserves that punishment." Women in the audience immediately and loudly protested Al-Razine's statement, and were shocked to learn the remarks came from a judge, the newspaper reported. Arab News reported that Al-Razine made his remark as he was attempting to explain why incidents of domestic violence had increased in Saudi Arabia. He said that women and men shared responsibility, but added that "nobody puts even a fraction of blame" on women, the newspaper said. Al-Razine "also pointed out that women's indecent behavior and use of offensive words against their husbands were some of the reasons for domestic violence in the country," it added. Domestic violence, which used to be a taboo subject in the conservative kingdom, has become a hot topic in recent years. Groups like the National Family Safety Program have campaigned to educate the public about the problem and help prevent domestic abuse. Saudi women's rights activist Wajeha Al-Huwaider told CNN that Saudi women routinely face such attitudes. "This is how men in Saudi Arabia see women," she said in a telephone interview from the Saudi city of Dahran. "It's not something they read in a book or learned from a friend. They've been raised to see women this way, that they're less than a person." Al-Huwaider added that "I'm not surprised to see a judge or a religious man saying that - they've been raised in the same culture - a culture that tells them it's ok to raise your hand to a woman that this works." Another Saudi judge, in the city of Onaiza, was the source of a separate recent controversy: he twice denied a request from the mother of an 8-year-old girl that the girl be granted a divorce from her 47-year-old husband. Last month, after human-groups condemned the union, the girl was granted the divorce.

outputs.L1:
(CNN) — Husbands are permitted to slap their wives if they spend lavishly, a Saudi judge recently said during a seminar on domestic violence, according to Saudi media reports published Sunday.

Judge Hamad Al-Razine told an audience that it was acceptable to slap Saudi women who spent excessively, Arab News, an English-language Saudi daily newspaper based in Riyadh, reported.

“If a person gives SR 1,200 [$320] to his wife and she spends 900 riyals [$240] to purchase an abaya [the black covering that women in Saudi Arabia must wear] from a brand shop, and if her husband slaps her on the face in reaction to her action, she deserves that punishment,” Al-Razine said.

Women in the audience immediately protested loudly and were shocked to learn that the remarks had come from a judge, the newspaper reported.

According to Arab News, Al-Razine made the remark while attempting to explain why incidents of domestic violence had increased in Saudi Arabia. He said that both women and men shared responsibility but added that “nobody puts even a fraction of blame” on women.

Al-Razine “also pointed out that women’s indecent behavior and use of offensive words against their husbands were some of the reasons for domestic violence in the country,” the newspaper added.

Domestic violence, once a taboo subject in the conservative kingdom, has become a prominent issue in recent years. Organizations such as the National Family Safety Program have campaigned to educate the public about the problem and help prevent domestic abuse.

Saudi women’s rights activist Wajeha Al-Huwaider told CNN that Saudi women routinely encounter such attitudes.

“This is how men in Saudi Arabia see women,” she said in a telephone interview from the Saudi city of Dahran. “It’s not something they read in a book or learned from a friend. They’ve been raised to see women this way—that they’re less than a person.”

Al-Huwaider added: “I’m not surprised to see a judge or a religious man saying that. They’ve been raised in the same culture—a culture that tells them it’s OK to raise your hand to a woman, that this works.”

Another Saudi judge, in the city of Onaiza, was at the center of a separate recent controversy after twice denying a mother’s request that her 8-year-old daughter be granted a divorce from her 47-year-old husband. Last month, after human rights groups condemned the union, the girl was granted the divorce.
outputs.L2:
(CNN) — A Saudi judge recently told a domestic-violence seminar that husbands may strike their wives for extravagant spending, according to Saudi media reports published Sunday.

Arab News, an English-language Saudi newspaper headquartered in Riyadh, reported that Judge Hamad Al-Razine offered an example involving a husband who gives his wife 1,200 Saudi riyals ($320). If she then uses 900 riyals ($240) to buy a designer abaya—the black garment Saudi women are required to wear—and her husband responds by slapping her face, Al-Razine said she merits the punishment.

Women attending the seminar immediately objected loudly. According to the newspaper, they were stunned that such comments had been made by a judge.

Arab News said Al-Razine made the statement while discussing the rise in domestic-violence cases in Saudi Arabia. Although he argued that both sexes bear responsibility, he also claimed that women receive virtually none of the blame. The paper added that he identified women’s supposedly improper conduct and their use of insulting language toward their husbands as factors contributing to domestic abuse in the country.

Once considered an unacceptable subject for public discussion in the conservative kingdom, domestic violence has drawn increasing attention in recent years. Organizations such as the National Family Safety Program have worked to raise public awareness and prevent abuse within families.

Saudi women’s rights campaigner Wajeha Al-Huwaider told CNN that women in the country regularly encounter views like Al-Razine’s. Speaking by telephone from Dahran, Saudi Arabia, she said Saudi men are brought up to regard women as less than fully human, rather than acquiring that belief from books or friends.

Al-Huwaider said she was not astonished to hear such words from a judge or religious figure because they were raised in the same society—a culture that teaches men that hitting women is acceptable and effective.

A different Saudi judge in Onaiza was also involved in a recent dispute. On two occasions, he rejected a mother’s appeal to have her 8-year-old daughter divorced from the girl’s 47-year-old husband. The divorce was ultimately granted last month after human-rights groups denounced the marriage.
outputs.L3:
Saudi judge Hamad Al-Razine sparked controversy during a seminar on domestic violence when he stated that a husband may slap his wife if she spends money excessively. To illustrate his argument, he cited the example of a woman purchasing an expensive abaya without sufficient justification.

The women attending the seminar reacted with loud protests and expressed shock that a judge would publicly endorse physical violence against a wife. Despite their objections, Al-Razine maintained that responsibility for the rise in domestic violence should be shared by both men and women. He suggested that, in some cases, women contribute to conflict through their behavior or the use of offensive language.

The remarks came amid growing public concern about domestic violence in Saudi Arabia. Organizations such as the National Family Safety Program have sought to increase awareness, support victims, and prevent abuse within families.

Women’s rights activist Wajeha Al-Huwaider criticized Al-Razine’s comments, arguing that they reflect deeply rooted social attitudes that portray Saudi women as inferior and normalize unequal treatment within marriage.
outputs.L4:
At a seminar in Saudi Arabia devoted to domestic violence, Judge Hamad Al-Razine provoked an angry reaction when he suggested that some wives might bring physical punishment upon themselves. While attempting to explain the reported rise in abuse, he cited examples such as a woman spending an excessive amount of household money on luxury items or behaving offensively toward her husband. In such circumstances, he argued, a husband might feel driven to slap his wife.

The remarks drew immediate protests from women in the audience and condemnation from women’s rights advocates. Critics said that financial disagreements, insults, or other marital conflicts could never justify physical violence. They also warned that blaming victims reinforces the social attitudes that prevent abused women from reporting attacks or seeking protection.

Advocates noted that domestic violence often remains hidden because victims fear family pressure, social stigma, or retaliation. When authority figures portray abuse as a reasonable response to a wife’s conduct, they argued, that message can further normalize violence and weaken efforts to hold abusers accountable.

The controversy exposed a broader tension in Saudi society. Public discussion of domestic abuse has increased, and activists have worked to secure greater recognition and protection for victims. Yet the judge’s comments demonstrated how deeply entrenched views about male authority and female obedience continue to shape attitudes toward marriage.

For campaigners, the incident underscored that confronting domestic violence requires more than seminars and public awareness programs. It also demands clear legal protections, effective enforcement, support services for victims, and a rejection of the idea that a woman’s behavior can make physical abuse acceptable.

### CNN Report Highlights Changing Roles of Husbands in Saudi Arabia

CNN has frequently reported on the social and economic changes taking place in Saudi Arabia. As the country modernizes, expectations surrounding marriage and the role of husbands are also evolving.

Traditionally, Saudi husbands were often viewed as the primary providers and decision-makers within their families. Today, however, more Saudi women are entering the workforce, pursuing higher education, and gaining greater independence. These developments have encouraged many couples to share financial responsibilities, household duties, and family decisions.

Despite significant reforms, experiences differ across Saudi society. Some families embrace more equal partnerships, while others continue to follow traditional customs. CNN’s coverage of Saudi Arabia often reflects this tension between rapid modernization and long-established cultural values.

The changing role of husbands is therefore part of a broader transformation in Saudi life—one shaped by government reforms, economic pressures, generational differences, and ongoing discussions about gender and family.

**Saudi Judge Draws Outcry Over Remarks Blaming Women for Domestic Violence**

**RIYADH, Saudi Arabia —** Saudi judge Hamad Al-Razine sparked controversy after suggesting that some women may be responsible for provoking violence by their husbands, remarks that drew protests from women attending a seminar on domestic abuse.

Speaking at a 2009 forum in Riyadh on the judiciary’s role in addressing domestic violence, Al-Razine offered the example of a wife who spent most of the money given to her on an expensive abaya, the traditional robe worn by Saudi women. He reportedly said that if her husband slapped her in response, she “deserved that punishment.”

Women in the audience objected loudly, according to reports in the Saudi press. Critics said the comments appeared to excuse physical abuse and shift responsibility from perpetrators to victims.

Al-Razine also acknowledged that domestic violence existed in Saudi Arabia, but argued that discussions of the issue should consider women’s behavior as well as men’s. His remarks intensified debate over the treatment of Saudi women and the ability of abuse victims to obtain protection through the courts.

Women’s-rights advocates said financial disagreements could never justify assault. They also warned that statements by judicial officials could discourage victims from reporting abuse, particularly in a legal and social system where women have historically faced obstacles in seeking protection or living independently.

The controversy came amid growing public scrutiny of domestic violence in the kingdom and calls for clearer laws and stronger safeguards. Saudi Arabia later adopted legislation criminalizing domestic abuse, though rights organizations have continued to raise concerns about enforcement and access to legal remedies.

counterfactuals.output:
Two 2009 incidents drew criticism of Saudi Arabia’s judiciary and treatment of women and girls:

- **Wife-slapping remarks:** Judge **Hamad al-Razine** told a domestic-violence seminar that a husband might be justified in slapping his wife if she spent excessively—for example, using most of the household money on an expensive abaya. Women’s-rights advocates condemned the remarks as victim-blaming and as legitimizing domestic abuse.

- **Child-bride divorce case:** A judge initially refused to annul the marriage of an **eight-year-old girl** to a man reported to be about **47–50 years old**. Her father had arranged the marriage, reportedly partly over financial matters. The judge ruled that the girl’s mother lacked standing and that the child could seek a divorce herself only after reaching puberty. Following public and human-rights pressure, the marriage was later dissolved.

Together, the controversies intensified debate over judicial discretion, male guardianship, domestic-violence protections, and Saudi Arabia’s then-lack of a clear minimum marriage age.
